sources.access_detail: open copy posted by the author (located 2026-09-25); a digital copy (available on request)
sources.quote: Burushaski has five short vowels: i, e, a, o, u, and five long bi-moraic ones: ii, ee, aa, oo, uu. The stress may fall on either of the two morae.
sources.locator: printed p. 165, sec. 1.10.2.2.1 Phonology, in the following chapter 1.10.2 'The Burushaski language' by Étienne Tiffou, not by Abbi
sources.note: Incidental: the only stress statement in the extract is in Tiffou's Burushaski chapter, which starts on the same printed page where Abbi's section ends. It states only that on bimoraic long vowels stress can sit on either mora (a contrast within long vowels), nothing on the position of word stress in general, secondary stress, weight or domain.The extract cuts off at p. 165 in mid-chapter.
sources.venue: The Languages and Linguistics of South Asia: A Comprehensive Guide

sources.citation: Smith, Alexander D. 2017. The Languages of Borneo: a comprehensive classification. PhD dissertation, University of Hawai'i at Manoa.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: not located online or in the libraries checked
sources.note: Nothing for Bulusu. Primary Bulusu data collected (consultant Sintang Pandi, Susua, Malinau; Appendix 9 Bulusu vocabulary pp. 636ff, no stress marks); stress is discussed only for Merap, Segai-Modang, Hliboi Bidayuh and other central-Borneo languages.

sources.citation: Lobel, Jason William. 2016. North Borneo Sourcebook: Vocabularies and Functors. (PALI Language Texts: Southeast Asia.) Honolulu: University of Hawai'i Press. xiv+288 pp.
sources.access_detail: open copy posted by the author (located 2026-09-25); a digital copy (available on request)
sources.locator: printed p. 1 (Introduction); Bulusu language-information page printed p. 55 (item 35); Bulusu rows in the wordlist section carry no stress, accent or length ma…
sources.note: Only modern published primary source with Bulusu data by a phonologically careful fieldworker; its introduction/transcription conventions may state whether stress is marked or predictable (penultimate) in the North Borneo languages including Bulusu. Wordlist-type work, so a stress statement is possible but not certain.

sources.citation: Lobel, Jason William. 2013. Philippine and North Bornean languages: issues in description, subgrouping, and reconstruction. PhD dissertation, University of Hawai'i at Manoa (hdl 10125/101972).
sources.note: Nothing for Bulusu. Bulusu appears only in ch. 11 'Southwest Sabah revisited' (pp. 359-360, 372, 393-394, 398 sec. 11.4.5) as a Murutic language of Kalimantan Timur and in functor/innovation tables (forms cited without accent marks). The only stress discussions are for Philippine languages (Manide/Alabat contrastive accent sec. 8.2.9; Maranao p. 287 fn. 3 'most languages native to Mindanao and areas further south have lost contrastive stress').

sources.citation: Lobel, Jason William. 2013. Southwest Sabah revisited. Oceanic Linguistics 52(1):36-68.
sources.note: Journal version of diss. ch. 11 (Glottolog's other Bulusu reference); content read in the dissertation and silent on stress, listed only for completeness in case the published version added transcription notes.

sources.citation: Appell, Amity C. P. 1986. The Bulusu' language of East Kalimantan: ethnographic profile and basic word list. Borneo Research Bulletin 18(2):166-175.
sources.note: Nothing. Ethnographic intro + c.250-item ANU Linguistic Atlas word list from one 19-year-old consultant (Imran, Tangap, Sekatak River); note 2: symbols follow Gudschinsky 1967, apostrophe = glottal stop. No stress marks, no prosodic statement.
